summary.title: Image Stitching with OpenCV and Python - PyImageSearch
summary.one_liner: You learn to stitch multiple overlapping images into a panorama using OpenCV's built-in Stitcher (cv2.createStitcher / cv2.Stitcher_create), and to crop away the black warp regions with a contour-and-erosion hack.
takeaways: OpenCV's built-in Stitcher (cv2.createStitcher in OpenCV 3, cv2.Stitcher_create in OpenCV 4) stitches a list of images in one call and returns a status code.
Stitcher status codes: OK=0, ERR_NEED_MORE_IMGS=1, ERR_HOMOGRAPHY_EST_FAIL=2, ERR_CAMERA_PARAMS_ADJUST_FAIL=3.
A simple script can stitch a folder of images in under 50 lines; warping leaves black regions around the panorama.
To crop black borders, threshold the stitched image, take the largest contour, then repeatedly erode a bounding rectangle until it contains no background pixels, and extract that ROI.

The built-in stitcher hides homography matrices, which makes it hard to convert into a real-time panorama pipeline; errors often come from using the wrong OpenCV version function name or missing contrib/non-free modules.
summary.summary: The tutorial shows how to stitch several overlapping photos into a panorama with OpenCV's built-in stitching function, based on the Brown and Lowe (2007) approach that handles image ordering, orientation, and illumination changes. It provides a simple script (image_stitching_simple.py) that loads a directory of images and calls the stitcher, then a second script (image_stitching.py) with an optional --crop flag. The crop method thresholds the result, finds the largest contour, and erodes a rectangle until it fits inside the panorama, removing black warp regions. The post also covers limitations, such as the built-in method hiding homography matrices, and common version and install errors.
